sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

RULE Dropping to 0 Hit Points:
When you drop to 0 hit points, you either die outright or fall unconscious, as explained in the following sections.

#### Instant Death

Massive damage can kill you instantly. When damage reduces you to 0 hit points and there is damage remaining, you die if the remaining damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum.

For example, a cleric with a maximum of 12 hit points currently has 6 hit points. If she takes 18 damage from an attack, she is reduced to 0 hit points, but 12 damage remains. Because the remaining damage equals her hit point maximum, the cleric dies.

#### Falling Unconscious

If damage reduces you to 0 hit points and fails to kill you, you fall unconscious (see appendix PH-A). This unconsciousness ends if you regain any hit points.

#### Death Saving Throws

Whenever you start your turn with 0 hit points, you must make a special saving throw, called a death saving throw, to determine whether you creep closer to death or hang onto life. Unlike other saving throws, this one isn't tied to any ability score. You are in the hands of fate now, aided only by spells and features that improve your chances of succeeding on a saving throw.

Roll a d20. If the roll is 10 or higher, you succeed. Otherwise, you fail. A success or failure has no effect by itself. On your third success, you become stable (see below). On your third failure, you die. The successes and failures don't need to be consecutive; keep track of both until you collect three of a kind. The number of both is reset to zero when you regain any hit points or become stable.

***Rolling 1 or 20.*** When you make a death saving throw and roll a 1 on the d20, it counts as two failures. If you roll a 20 on the d20, you regain 1 hit point.

***Damage at 0 Hit Points.*** If you take any damage while you have 0 hit points, you suffer a death saving throw failure. If the damage is from a critical hit, you suffer two failures instead. If the damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum, you suffer instant death.

#### Stabilizing a Creature

The best way to save a creature with 0 hit points is to heal it. If healing is unavailable, the creature can at least be stabilized so that it isn't killed by a failed death saving throw.

You can use your action to administer first aid to an unconscious creature and attempt to stabilize it, which requires a successful DC 10 Wisdom (Medicine) check.

A **stable** creature doesn't make death saving throws, even though it has 0 hit points, but it does remain unconscious. The creature stops being stable, and must start making death saving throws again, if it takes any damage. A stable creature that isn't healed regains 1 hit point after 1d4 hours.

#### Monsters and Death

Most GMs have a monster die the instant it drops to 0 hit points, rather than having it fall unconscious and make death saving throws.

Mighty villains and special nonplayer characters are common exceptions; the GM might have them fall unconscious and follow the same rules as player characters.

At the end of a long rest, a character regains all lost hit points. The character also regains spent Hit Dice, up to a number of dice equal to half of the character's total number of them (minimum of one die). For example, if a character has eight Hit Dice, he or she can regain four spent Hit Dice upon finishing a long rest.

A character can't benefit from more than one long rest in a 24-hour period, and a character must have at least 1 hit point at the start of the rest to gain its benefits.

Pell wakes while you work, a lanky lad with his mother's jaw, and watches the torn edges of his arm knit together under your hand as if it were happening to someone else. The village comes in bit by bit once the news runs door to door. Dobb Harrow is the first: a heavy, quiet man with Cal's family's shoulders, and he takes the longbow from you without a word and holds it a long while. Then you ask about the cut bank.

You go to the lip with the rope looped at your waist and Hennet and Marl braced behind you, and you hold your breath and listen. Perception (10): you hear the stream, a crow, the creak of the rope, and not much else. A pebble dropped from your hand ticks down the slope and rolls to a stop, and nothing answers it. The dark gives you nothing either way. It is as quiet as a well.

Then the work starts, and it goes the way you ordered. Hennet and Marl hold the ropes, the Fenner cousins stand ready on the sledge, Dobb sets the bar under the slab, and you stand at the edge with your shield facing the mouth, saying nothing, watching the black. Dobb grunts a count, and the beam bites, and the slab shifts with a groan like a tooth being drawn.

Athletics (13), by the narrowest margin: it goes. The slab drops with a dull roar. Dirt and root-ends and a rain of loose stone come down across the opening in a gray cloud, and the lads scramble back, coughing. When the dust thins, the mouth is mostly gone, buried under a rough heap of earth and slabs, but the old roof was rotten along the north lip, as it turns out. A ragged gap about two feet wide is still open at the top corner, black and cold, breathing out the same sour draught.

Then, as the last of the dust settles, you hear it: a thin dry scratching from far below, slow and patient, like a nail drawn along stone. It stops. It starts again.

It is a little past 11 in the morning. The oil jug sits unopened, there is still a good beam, and the lads are watching you with white faces. Dobb says quietly, "That'll not hold a thing that wants out. Another hour with rubble, if we start now."

What does Brannoc do?

"Then another hour it is, and we don't stop until it's shut tight. Hennet, Marl, haul rubble to the gap; Dobb and the Fenner cousins, wedge the beam across it and pack stones and earth over that."

"Pour the oil down the gap first, Dobb, a good soaking, then drop a lit rag after it. Fire and light are what they fear, and it may buy us the time. I'll stand at the lip with my shield, and if that scratching grows louder, everyone drops the tools and runs for the road."

Your plain answers first: yes, you couldn't act, and nothing could wake you. At 0 HP you stay unconscious until you regain hit points, and water or a touch on the amulet won't do that. Hennet did drag you back from the gap, and he put a hand to your throat and your side and stabilized you with his first aid. It is the reason you are alive. Here is the rest of the afternoon, which you did not see.

The ghoul came out of the gap as the beam slid. Its claws took Marl before he could turn, a single stroke, and he fell. You went in with your mace and struck true, and it was Dobb's iron bar, swung on a lucky, wild blow, that took it hard in the ribs. Then its claws found you twice, and you fell. Hennet pulled you clear, saved your life, and was killed where he knelt. Dobb followed him. The two Fenner cousins fought on with a pick and a sledge, and they hurt it badly, but they were farm lads, and they died there too.

When the dust settled, the thing was left with three hit points, a ruined body, and the dead around it. It did not touch you. It took one of the bodies by the collar, dragged it back through the gap, and went down into the dark.

You wake at 3 in the afternoon, with the sun slanting through the roots, one hit point, and no prayers. The beam sits crooked across the open gap. The iron bar lies in the dirt, bent. Cal's longbow is where Dobb left it. And the grass around the cut is trodden and red. Five men of Hollow Reach died here at your word: Marl, Hennet, Dobb Harrow, and the two Fenner cousins, Wat and Ned. You didn't see it, and you can't unsee it now.

The gap is still open. Behind you the village waits with no word of what has happened. Your next long rest can't count until about midnight, so you have no spells until tomorrow, and you have 1 HP, a Hit Die, a mace, and a shield.

What does Brannoc do?

I bow my head over the bodies, and say the prayer for the dead over Dobb, Hennet, Marl, and Wat and Ned, because they followed my plan and I will carry that. "Rest easy. I'll bring you home, and I'll tell your families the truth."

Then I spend my Hit Die and bind what I can, and with the wounded ghoul at three hit points and afraid of light, I'll pour what lamp oil is left and put a lit lantern in the gap to hold it shut until I can rest. You wait an hour at the cut. It is the right word for it, because you pray more than you rest. You lay the four of them out in a row with their coats over their faces, Dobb and Hennet and Marl and Wat, and say the old words over each, your voice rough, humming where the words give out. Ned's coat lies empty where the thing took him. The hour passes in a slow, ragged peace. You finish it at 9 hit points, stiff, scraped raw, and with the sun leaning west.

To your questions:

Yes, someone left something behind. Dobb's hooded lantern lies on its side near the bent iron bar, dented but whole, and Hennet's satchel, torn across the strap, holds a pint flask of lamp oil and a rag. It is not much, but it is something.

Yes, the trail is easy to read. A smeared dark furrow runs from the dirt at the gap's lip down into the scree, the heel-marks of a body dragged, and beside it a ghoul's long-fingered handprints, with a drop of black blood every pace. It leads straight into the opening and down.

You do as you said. You right the lantern, trim the wick, and light it from your tinderbox. You pour the pint of oil into its reservoir and wedge it in the crooked beam above the gap, where the flame stands steady and gold in the afternoon light. Nothing stirs below. The air that breathes out of the hole still smells sour, but the flame leans only a little.

It is almost 4 in the afternoon. The lantern will burn a few hours at best, not the night. You have 9 HP and no prayers until midnight, five dead men to bring home, and the village still waits for word. The light will fail well before the ghouls wake.

What does Brannoc do?

I check the beam one last time, then wrap the four bodies in their coats and tie them onto the handcart Dobb's folk left, with Cal's longbow laid beside them. "I'll bring you home. Then I'll tell the Widow and the Fenners the truth, and ask for every lantern in Hollow Reach to be lit at the Lamp track and the barn tonight."

I haul the cart toward the village, shield on my arm, mace ready, keeping to the sunlit road. DM: the gap's lantern won't last the night, so is there a way to keep it burning, and is there any trace of Ned's body or the ghoul's wound that suggests how long it will stay down?

Keeping the light burning: the lantern has one pint of oil, which will last a few hours but not the night. You have ten candles, and each burns for one hour, shedding bright light in a 5-foot radius and dim light for another 5 feet. Ned's body and the wound: the drag-trail goes down the scree and into the dark at an angle, and you can see only about twenty feet of it before it vanishes under the roof. Three hit points are a sliver of life, and the thing is not hurt in the way a wolf would be. It will not bleed out, and the wound will not stop it hunting at dusk. You cannot tell how long it will stay down. You have to assume it is awake the moment the light fails.

You tie the four of them onto Dobb's handcart with their coats tight around them, lay Cal's longbow beside, and take up the shafts. The wheels creak, and the cart drags heavy in the dust. The sun is long and gold, and the stubble fields stretch off to the south. It takes half an hour of slow, aching walking.

At the edge of Hollow Reach the dogs bark once, and then people come out, one door at a time, women with their sleeves still floury, two old men, children held back by the wrist. They see the cart, and the coats, and the shield on your arm, and they stop. Nobody says anything. A girl of eight or nine looks at Hennet's boots on the end of the cart and begins very quietly to cry.

Then Widow Harrow comes along the road from the barn, wiping her hands, and sees your face and slows. Behind her, limping on a crutch with Tam at his elbow, comes Joss Fenner, and he looks at the cart a long moment. At the shape of Wat and Ned's coat he makes a small, broken sound.

It is the hour you promised yourself: the truth. They are waiting, and you have not said a word. How does Brannoc tell them?

I stop the cart, set down the shafts, and take off my helm so they can see my face. "Widow Harrow, Joss, all of you: these four followed my plan this morning, and they died for it. Dobb, Hennet, Marl, and Wat are here, and Ned was taken below by the thing we failed to seal. I won't dress it up. It was my word that sent them, and I'm sorry."

I look at Joss and Tam and kneel in the road beside the cart. "I can't give them back. But I can tell you how they fought: Dobb struck it with the iron bar, Hennet pulled me out of the dark and saved my life, and the cousins stood their ground when they could have run. The thing is hurt, with three hit points left, and the gap is lit but won't hold the night. Whatever you decide, I'll stand with you tonight, and I'll ask for every lantern and all the oil Hollow Reach can spare."

When you finish, the silence has a weight, and the only sound is the little girl, still crying, quiet as a kitten.

Joss lets go of his crutch. He stands a moment longer than he should, because he is a big man and does not want to be seen wavering. Then he limps to the cart, lays a hand on the coat over Wat, and bows his head. Tam presses against his father's side. Nobody speaks.

The first voice comes from the crowd and it is not kind. A woman pushes through, a hard-faced woman in a flour-white apron, with Wat's chin. Berra Fenner. "You said it'd be sealed by dark. You said." Her hands are shaking. "Two sons. I had two." She does not strike you, though for a moment you think she will. Then she sags against Joss's arm, and the anger runs out of her and there is only the other thing.

It is Widow Harrow who speaks into that. "He came back," she says, low, and her voice is steady. "That's what the others didn't do, the ones who rode through in the spring and didn't stop. He walked in at the door and he told us. He sat with my boy a night and a day when he could have run for the road." She looks at you, and at the cart, and at the others. "We lost five good men. We'd have lost every soul in that barn."

Joss nods slowly. "We'll bring them home," he says, "and then we'll finish it. Every lantern in the Reach, and every jar of oil. I've got three in my cellar." Berra says nothing, but she turns and walks stiffly back toward her door, and a moment later two of the women follow her in. She comes out again with a jug, and she sets it on the cart's tail without looking at you.

By half past four the village is a different place: people quiet, hands busy, doors open. You are at 9 HP and still have no prayers. Dusk comes in about two hours, and the gap is lit but won't hold the night. Old Garrit has said there is stone in the Fenner quarry cut and a team of oxen that can drag a slab. Joss says four hands could put it over the gap before dark, but he cannot go himself, and every strong young man the Reach had is lying in a row on a cart.

What does Brannoc do?

I bow my head to Berra Fenner. "Goodwife, I'll carry your sons' names as long as I live." Then I turn to Old Garrit and Joss. "I'll take the oxen and the slab, with every able hand left, women and the older boys too, and we set it over the gap before dusk."

"Have the rest gather every lantern and jar of oil and set them around the barn and the Long Cut. Pell and Dorrin, you're mended, so I'll have you with me, and I'll keep the crossbow loaded and the lamp lit until the slab is down."

You climb the track in clear noon light, past the bracken and the beeches that held such dread two nights ago. The lamp-house is smaller by day, a squat gray building, its door open and the iron lamp steady in its dusk-pale flame on the plinth. The flagstone in the floor is shut tight, and there is a new scorch mark at its edge where something clawed from below and gave up. Hob sits on the step as he sat in the night, lantern in his lap. He lifts his head slowly when your shadow falls across him.

You tell him all of it: Nessa Tarn and the oil, Pell and Dorrin and Old Garrit and the rota, and that you are going to Greywater to carry word to Maud. He is quiet so long that you think he has not understood. Then his dry voice comes up, careful, like a man lifting something heavy.

"...Maud. Tell her... I kept the light. Tell her I was not... afraid. At the end." The lantern turns in his hands. "There is a shawl. Blue. She wove it, the winter I came here. It is in the chest... there." His chin lifts toward the corner of the lamp-house. "She is to have it back. Tell her it was warm. Every night. Tell her that."

He says nothing for a while. Then, as an afterthought: "She talks... too much. She will say I should have come home. Tell her... I had somewhere to be."

Answering your other question: the chest holds spare wicks and a flint, and the lamp is full. Oil is the real need, and Nessa and Berra have promised it. Your candles would only be a spare for a bad night, and ten would be a kindness. They are yours to leave or keep.

It is a little past noon. Greywater is a day's walk. If you leave now at a steady pace you will arrive after dark, around nine, and the valley road is not one you know. What does Brannoc do?

I fetch the blue shawl from the chest, fold it carefully into my pack, and leave five of my ten candles on the step beside Hob. "Five for a bad night, and I'll keep five for the road. I'll tell Maud every word: that you kept the light, that you weren't afraid, that the shawl was warm, and that you had somewhere to be."

Then I say goodbye with a hand on his cold shoulder and set out down the valley road at a steady pace, shield on my arm, Protection from Evil and Good ready. You remember Hob's words exactly, because you turned them over all the way down the road. He said:

"Tell her I kept the light. Tell her I was not afraid, at the end. There is a shawl, blue. She wove it the winter I came here. She is to have it back. Tell her it was warm, every night." And last, a little wryly: "She talks too much. She will say I should have come home. Tell her I had somewhere to be."

As for what you say first to Maud, that is yours to decide, but the simple truth is probably kindest. You could say your name and that you come from Hob, and that the shawl is in your pack, before you tell her the harder thing.

The road goes by without trouble. The valley is a slow curve of stubble fields, hedgerows hung with red hips, and a river glinting on your left. You pass a goatherd who nods and a tinker's cart going the other way, and nobody who needs a healer. You hum the whole way, and a boy fishing the bank stops to listen.

At ten to seven, with the sun low and gold behind you, the Millstone Inn comes up out of the river mist: a big old mill of gray stone, its waterwheel still turning, lamps lit in every window, smoke rising from two chimneys. A wide yard, a stable, and a signboard with a millstone painted on it hang over the door.

You step into the common room and the warmth hits you. It is clean and full of the smell of bread and onions. A stout woman with her sleeves rolled to the elbow looks you up and down, mace, shield, and amulet, and says, "Healer? Gods be thanked. Hesper Cole. I've a carter's boy in the back room with a cough that's been going on three days, and he's going the wrong way. Will you look at him? Bed and supper are yours, either way."

What does Brannoc do?

"Of course, Hesper. Take me to him, and bring a lamp and a cup of warm water with a little honey if you have it."

I'll kneel by the boy, listen to his breathing and feel his forehead and throat, and ask how long the cough has run, whether he's bringing up anything, and whether anyone else in the inn is sick. If it's more than I can ease with Medicine and rest, I'll use Cure Wounds or Healing Word as it fits.

Hesper leads you through the kitchen to a narrow back room with a pallet under the eaves. Her lamp falls across a boy of about nine, flushed and sweat-damp, his hair stuck flat to his forehead. His name is Piper, and he does not stir when you kneel. His cough is wet and deep, and between spells his breath whistles.

Medicine (8): you don't get a clear read. His forehead is hot, his throat is rough, and the cough is plainly wet, but you cannot tell whether this is a bad chill that has settled low or something worse. His chest sounds muddy under your ear, but the pulse and the heat don't settle it either way, and you are honestly unsure.

What you do learn from asking is this. Hesper says the cough started three days ago, that he brings up a thick yellow-gray phlegm in the morning, and that no one else in the inn is sick. His father, Garn the carter, left him here and went on to Greywater with a load of cloth, and is due back in two days. The boy has taken little but water and broth.

You warm honey-water at the kitchen fire, and lift Piper to sip it. He takes half the cup and dozes off against your arm. Steam from a kettle in the room loosens his breath a little. Nothing you can do tonight will cure it outright, and Cure Wounds mends wounds, not fevers, so you hold it back.

It's about twenty past seven. Supper is on the table, Hesper has a free bed for you, and the boy is not worse, though he is not better. You could sit up with him, check him through the night, ask more of Hesper, or try a different approach tomorrow.

What does Brannoc do?

I eat a quick supper, then bring a stool to Piper's bedside and keep the kettle steaming. "Hesper, would you prop his shoulders up with a rolled blanket and wake me if his breathing changes? I'll sit with him tonight, since I promised never to let anyone suffer alone."

I'll check his breathing and brow every hour or so, humming low. DM: does Piper have a fever I could cool with a damp cloth, and can I try Medicine again with more time, or does anything in the room, like the phlegm or his lips, give me a clearer read?

transcript.text: notebook: updated Piper

You eat Hesper's onion-and-barley stew, standing, and are back at the boy's side before the bowl is cold. Hesper props his shoulders on a rolled blanket without a word. She has done this before, for her own, and she says as much with a look. Then she leaves you the lamp and the kettle and tells you to knock on the wall if you need her.

Yes, he has a fever. His brow is hot and dry, and a cloth wrung in cool water takes the edge off it for a quarter of an hour at a time. You change it as it warms.

Medicine (13), a second look with hours of watching behind it: this time it comes clear. His lips are faintly blue-gray at the edges whenever the cough hits, and his breath takes a catch at the top of each inhalation, a small hitch. The phlegm in the cup is thick and rust-colored, not the pale spit of a cold. You are fairly sure now. This is a fever settled in the lungs, a true chest sickness, not a chill and not a wound. It is a fight his body has to win, with help. It is also why Cure Wounds was never going to touch it, and why Lesser Restoration, which ends a disease, would. It is a 2nd-level spell, and you cannot cast it until level 3.

What you can do is keep him upright, keep him cool, give him steam and honey water in small sips, and watch the breath. You do all of it through the night, humming low. Around the middle of the night his breathing eases from a rasp to a rattle, and a little before one o'clock his brow cools under your hand and a thin sweat breaks across it. He sleeps properly for the first time. He is not out of danger, but the worst of the climb is behind him.

It is twenty past midnight on Day 4. You are tired but steady. In a few hours Greywater's weaver will be waiting, and you may sleep for a while before the road, or stay longer with Piper.

What does Brannoc do?

I lay a hand on Piper's damp brow and let out a long breath. "Sleep well, little one." I'll get a few hours of rest on the stool beside him, then wake at first light to check his breathing once more before the road.

In the morning I'll tell Hesper plainly what the sickness is: keep him upright, cool, and sipping honey water, and send for a healer if the blue returns to his lips. I'll also leave a note for Garn the carter that his boy is mending and that Brannoc of Hollow Reach sat with him. Then I'll set out for Greywater with the shawl and Hob's words.

Your answer first: Healing Word restores hit points and nothing else, so it can't ease a fever or a bad chest. The sickness is not a wound. You can cast it and give him a little more strength for the road, but it wouldn't touch what is wrong, and I won't pretend it would. Your slots are better kept. The sleep, steam, and honey water are doing the real work.

You settle on the stool with your back against the wall, your hand where you can feel his breath. You sleep, in snatches, for six hours or so. Hesper wakes you at first gray with a mug of hot tea. Piper is awake and watching you with big, clear eyes. His fever has dropped to a mild warmth, his breath comes slow and mostly quiet, and he asks, hoarse, whether you are the man who hummed. You say you are. He says it helped, and goes back to sleep.

You tell Hesper plainly what it is: a sickness settled in the chest. Keep him upright, keep him cool, keep honey water in him in small sips, and send for a healer if the blue ever comes back to his lips. You write a few lines in the margin of a page of your prayer book, tear it neatly out, and leave it under the lamp for Garn: your son is mending, and Brannoc of Hollow Reach sat with him. Hesper refuses your coin and presses a heel of bread and a hard cheese into your hands. "Bed and board's for them as earn it," she says. "You did."

By seven you are on the road with the shawl in your pack. The mist lies thick on the river, and the sun is pale behind it. The road goes through low hills and pastures grazed gray-green, past a ford and a ruined chapel with its roof fallen in. It is quiet, and your steps and your humming are the only sound.

At about nine, the road bends and Greywater comes into view below, a cluster of slate roofs along the river, with racks of dyed wool drying red and blue and ochre in rows along the bank, and a weir turning white across the water. A small chapel stands at the near end with its door shut. A girl hauling a basket of yarn looks up, sees you, and stops. At the lower end of the village, by the weir, there is a house with a blue door.

What does Brannoc do?

I nod to the girl and ask gently, "Good morning. Could you tell me where Maud Marrow the weaver lives? I've come with word of her brother."

Then I walk down to the house with the blue door, shield slung on my back so I look less like a soldier, and knock. When she opens, I'll say, "Maud Marrow? My name is Brannoc, and I come from Hob. May I come in? I have something of yours in my pack, and I'd like to tell you about him in my own words."

input.add_to_description: Day 4 ~9:20 AM: Brannoc reached her blue-door loom-house in Greywater with the shawl and Hob's words. transcript.result: added to Maud Marrow's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Maud Marrow

The girl with the yarn basket points without a word at the blue door, then crosses herself, a gesture of the old kind, and goes back to her work more slowly than before. You slip your shield onto your back, as you said, and walk down past the dye racks. The air smells of wet wool, woad, and wood smoke. The weir runs loud beside you.

The blue door is faded, the paint worn pale at the latch. From inside comes the steady knock and slide of a loom, a rhythm that has gone on so long it has become a kind of silence. You knock, and the sound stops.

The door opens on a lean woman in her sixties with a long gray braid, a leather apron, and fingertips stained blue to the second joint. She has Hob's long jaw and Hob's pale, patient eyes, but hers are quick and sharp. She looks at your amulet, at the mud on your boots, and at the way you are standing, and the color leaves her face before you have said a word.

You say it as you planned. Your name, that you come from Hob, that you have something of hers in your pack, and that you would tell her about him in your own words.

"Come in," she says, very quietly. She holds the door and steps back. The room is warm and crowded with wool and half-finished cloth, a great loom by the window, a kettle on the hob, and a single chair pulled up beside the fire, empty, with a folded blanket over its arm. She does not sit. She stands with both hands pressed flat on the back of the other chair.

"He's dead," she says. It is not a question. "Isn't he. I knew in the spring, when he went up that track and wouldn't be told. I said, 'Hob, you'll die in that damned lamp-house and nobody'll know for a month.'" Her voice cracks on the last word and steadies. "Say it. Say it plain, and then give me what you've got in that pack."

She is waiting. You have the shawl, Hob's words, and the whole of what happened. How does Brannoc tell her?

I take off my pack, set it on the table, and meet her eyes. "Yes, Maud. Hob died some time before the harvest feast, in the lamp-house, and nobody found him. I won't dress it up. But he did not leave the light, and he was not alone at the end: he kept it burning, and he saved a village by it."

I take out the blue shawl and hold it out in both hands. "He asked me to give you this. He said you wove it the winter he went up there, and I'm to tell you it was warm every night. He said to tell you he kept the light, that he wasn't afraid at the end." I add gently, "And he said you'd tell him he should have come home. He asked me to say he had somewhere to be."

sheet: lost 1 × Blue shawl (Maud Marrow's, to return to her); XP +100: 400

Maud does not move while you speak. When you reach the part about the light, her mouth tightens, and at "somewhere to be" something goes out of her, all at once, like a thread cut. She takes the shawl from you with both hands. For a moment she only holds it, thumbs moving over the weave, over a place near the hem where the pattern wanders.

"I dropped a stitch there," she says. "He used to say he liked it. Said it was the only part of it that was honestly mine and not the pattern's." She laughs, wetly, once. Then she sits down in the empty chair by the fire, with the blue wool bundled against her chest, and weeps like a woman who has put off weeping for half a year.

You do not hurry her, and you do not speak. You sit on the stool by the hearth with your hands loose between your knees, and when the kettle starts to sing you rise and take it off. You find the cups, and you pour. It is not much. It is what Edda would have done. She takes the cup without looking at it, and her hand is steady.

Some time later, perhaps an hour, she asks the questions. Did it hurt? You tell her you don't believe so. Was he alone? Not at the end, you say, and she does not ask more than that. She asks about the village, and you tell her about the Reach and the barn, about Cal and the others, and the five candles on the step. She listens with her chin on the shawl.

At last she wipes her face with her sleeve and looks at you with Hob's steady eyes in a living face. "Then I'll go up to him," she says. "Not today. I've work due, and a body can't go anywhere in this state. Within the week. I'll bring wool and a loom-stool and sit with the old fool until he tells me to go home." She nods slowly. "You'll tell them at the Reach to expect a woman who talks too much."

She presses your hand between both of hers, stained fingers warm. She will not take coin, or let you go without a loaf and a jar of honey from her shelf. Your XP stands at 400, and the shawl is where it belongs.

It is a quarter to eleven on Day 4. You are fed, rested, and full of prayers, with fifteen gold pieces and no one waiting on you. Hollow Reach has its rota, Hob has his sister, and the road runs on in two directions. The chapel at Greywater has no priest, and a girl with a yarn basket looked at you with a particular hope.

What does Brannoc do?

I thank Maud, take the loaf and honey, and tell her, "I'll tell the Reach to expect a woman who talks too much, and Hob will be glad of it." Then I walk up to the little chapel at the near end of the village and look for the girl with the yarn basket, to ask her who tends it now and who in Greywater has been sick or hurt with no healer to turn to.

input.description: Girl of about twelve in Greywater, a dyer's daughter who hauls yarn baskets and sweeps the village's priestless chapel. Hopeful and direct. Tells Brannoc the chapel has had no priest since the old one died two winters ago; the sick are tended by the weavers as best they can.

Level 3 needs 900 XP, and you have 400, so you need 500 more. At 3rd level you would gain two 2nd-level slots, and Lesser Restoration is a Life domain spell for 3rd level. That means it would be always prepared and wouldn't count against your limit. It ends one disease or one condition (blinded, deafened, paralyzed, or poisoned), so it would have broken Piper's lung fever outright, and it would end a ghoul's paralysis on you or an ally.

You thank Maud once more, and she gives your hand a last squeeze and shoos you out. The loaf and a jar of honey go into your pack, and you walk up the lane, past the racks of drying wool, to the chapel.

It is a small slate-roofed building with a bell-cote and no bell. The door is unlocked. Inside it is swept clean, with wildflowers in a jar on a plain stone altar, and nobody in sight. The girl from the lane is standing on the step behind you, the yarn basket on her hip. Her name is Wren, a dyer's daughter of twelve or so, and she looks at you directly.

"Old Father Tulle died two winters back," she says. "Nobody's come since. I sweep it, because somebody should." She hesitates. "People still come to sit. When they're frightened."

She tells you who is ill, when you ask, and she's thorough about it. Three people in Greywater are suffering with no one to see to them. A weaver named Osric has a scalded forearm that never closed and is going red at the edges. A woman named Ilsa Dunmore has been coughing for a fortnight, and her baby has the same rattle. And old Perrin Gale, who dyes in the sheds, fell from a rack and hasn't walked straight since, and he won't let anyone look at it.

You have all three prayers ready, three 1st-level slots, and Channel Divinity. It is a little past eleven in the morning. You could see all three, or only one first.

What does Brannoc do?

"Thank you, Wren. Will you take me to Osric first? A scald going red at the edges won't wait, and I'll see Ilsa and her baby next, then Perrin, who I'll ask kindly rather than force."

I'll start with Medicine to clean and look at the burn, and use Cure Wounds only if it needs more than clean linen and honey. I'll keep a slot for Perrin's fall and ask Wren to come along and tell him I'm a friend of Maud Marrow's.

Brannoc cleaned it, drew the matter with a honey dressing and linen, and judged it will heal without magic if kept clean and changed daily. Taught Wren to change the dressing.

Wren leads you along the river to a long dye-shed where Osric sits on an overturned tub with his arm wrapped in a filthy rag. He is a thick-armed man, gray at the temples, and he eyes you warily until Wren says you are a friend of Maud Marrow's. After that, he lets you unwind the cloth.

Medicine (17): the forearm tells you everything. It is a deep scald, three weeks old, split in two places along the inner arm, and angry red at the margins, with a little yellow weeping. It smells faintly sour. The flesh is hot but not black, there are no red streaks running toward the elbow, and he has no fever. It is festering, not rotting. You are confident it will mend without magic if it is kept clean.

You do what it needs. You wash it with warm salt water, trim the dead skin back to the clean edge with the small knife from your pack, and spread honey thin over the raw places, honey from Maud's own jar. Then you wrap it in clean linen, firmly but not tight. Osric swears through his teeth and does not pull away. You show Wren how to change the dressing each morning and each night, with boiled water and fresh honey, and she nods gravely and repeats every step back to you.

"It'll close in a fortnight," you tell him. "Keep it out of the vats. If the red climbs above the wrist, or you take a fever, send for me." He nods, a little humbled. "Thank you," he says gruffly. "I'd about decided to lose the arm."

You saved your slot. It is a quarter to noon. Wren takes you next to a low house on the village's east lane, where a thin, tired woman stands in the doorway with a baby on her shoulder. You hear the rattle in the baby's chest from three paces away. This is Ilsa Dunmore.

What does Brannoc do?

I smile at Ilsa and keep my voice soft. "Goodwife, I'm Brannoc, a friend of Maud Marrow's. May I come in and listen to the little one's chest, and to yours? I'll ask how long you've both been coughing, and whether the baby is feeding."

Inside I'll sit her by the fire and check the baby's lips for blue, the fever, and the breathing, then use Medicine with honey-water, steam and propped sleeping, as with Piper. DM: Ilsa's husband, if there is one, and how old is the baby?

Ilsa lets you in with a tired, grateful nod. She is perhaps twenty-three, hollow under the eyes, and when she says her husband's name it is with the care of someone not letting herself miss him too much. Garrick Dunmore is a boatman, upriver hauling dyestuffs, due back in about four days. The baby is Tessa, a girl of four months, round-faced and flushed, with a damp little fist knotted in her mother's collar.

You sit Ilsa by the fire, and you ask, and you listen.

Medicine (16): the picture comes clear enough. Ilsa's cough is dry and deep, of a fortnight's standing, with an ache under the ribs and a night sweat. It is a lingering chest cold that never quite cleared, made worse by tiredness and a smoky, closed room. It's not the lung fever Piper had. The baby's breath is rapid but not labored, and the rattle is wet and loose, not tight. Her lips are pink, she is feeding, and she has no fever above warmth. Tessa has caught her mother's cough, and is likely to mend as her mother mends.

What would help most is plain. You have Ilsa lie back with her shoulders propped, and you give her warm honey-water in sips, and you show her how to keep the baby upright against her chest when she sleeps. You open the shutter a hand's breadth to let the smoke out. You show her how to steam a kettle by the bed. You leave a third of Maud's honey, and you tell her to eat when she can and to send Wren for you at once if Tessa's lips go blue, if she won't feed, or if she turns hot and still. It is not magic. It is the kind of care that was missing, and she cries a little with the relief of having someone say plainly that her baby is not dying.

You spend nothing from your slots. It is twenty-five to one. Perrin Gale is waiting in the dye-sheds, the one who won't let anyone look at his fall, and Wren stands in the lane with her basket, watching you.

What does Brannoc do?

"Thank you, Wren. Take me to Perrin, and tell him on the way that I'm a friend of Maud's and I only want to look, not to fuss."

At the dye-sheds I'll keep my distance, sit on an upturned tub where he can see my hands, and talk about the work first, how long he's dyed and what colors, before asking how he fell and what hurts. I'll offer to look at his back or leg only if he agrees, and I'll keep Cure Wounds ready in case it's a true injury.

input.description: Old dyer of Greywater, proud and gruff, who fell from a drying rack a month ago and has walked crooked since; won't let anyone look at it. Brannoc won his trust by asking about the dye work. Injury: left hip and lower back; Brannoc's first read inconclusive (Medicine 8). DM ruling: Cure Wounds restores hit points only and cannot unset an old crooked injury.

transcript.result: entry Perrin Gale (person) created; relationship [34] added to Perrin Gale

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Perrin Gale; added 1 relationship to Perrin Gale

Wren walks ahead of you on the way down and tells Perrin from the shed door that you are a friend of Maud Marrow's and want only to look. The old man grumbles from the dark inside that he has seen enough healers to last a hundred years, and none of them ever came to a clean thing.

You do as you planned. You sit on an upturned tub where he can see your hands, rest the mace and shield against the wall, and say nothing about his fall. You ask about his dyes instead: how long he has been at it, what the madder does that the woad cannot, where he gets his weld. He is a long time answering, and then he cannot stop. He has been dyeing for fifty-one years, and he knows the river's moods like a woman's. Persuasion (17): by the time his hands have stopped tightening on the tub's edge, he is the one who says it, gruffly, to the vat. "Fell from the rack. Third rung. A month back."

He lets you look, once you ask, and only as far as he will.

Medicine (8): you can't make a clear read of it. He winces when you press his left hip and lower back, and the hip sits a little higher than the right, as if the whole frame has set at a slant. You can't tell whether it's a deep bruise that has knotted the muscle, a hip knocked out of its seat and left, or a cracked bone that healed crooked. He walks on it, and he won't go to bed. Each would need something different.

One thing you can say. Cure Wounds restores hit points, and by my ruling it does not unset a month-old hurt that has already healed wrong. It could ease the wearing damage, but it would not make a crooked hip straight. You have all three slots, though, and you could spend one if you want to try anyway.

It's about twenty past one. Perrin is watching you with wary, tired eyes. Wren is perched on a drying rack, quiet for once.

What does Brannoc do?

"Master Perrin, I can't promise to straighten what's healed crooked, but I can try to ease the ache and the wear on that hip. May I lay a hand on it and say a short prayer? It won't hurt, and it costs you nothing."

If he agrees, I'll cast Cure Wounds on him at 1st level and see what it does. Either way, I'll show him a gentle stretch, and ask him to keep a stool at his vat so he isn't standing all day. DM: is there a bonesetter or surgeon in Greywater or nearby I could send him to for the hip itself?

input.add_to_description: Day 4 ~1:50 PM: agreed to a prayer; Cure Wounds eased the ache. Hip still sits crooked. Brannoc showed him a stretch and told him to keep a stool at the vat; recommended Mother Aldith of Stonebridge.

transcript.result: added to Perrin Gale's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Perrin Gale

He is silent for a moment. Then he gives a short, grudging nod, the nod of a man agreeing to a thing he plainly thinks is foolish. "Say your prayer, then. Mind the hip."

You kneel and lay a hand on the small of his back, over the knotted muscle, and say it low. The warmth gathers and goes in. It is not a great working, and you can feel it spread through the band of tightness and then stop at the place where the bone sits wrong, like water finding a wall. Ten points of life go into him. Perrin draws a long breath through his nose, shoulders dropping an inch, and lets it out slowly.

"Well," he says. "That's the first night I'd sleep through in a month."

The hip itself is unchanged. When he stands, it still sits a little high, and he still carries it with the same cautious lean. But the grinding wince has gone out of his face. You show him a gentle stretch, one knee drawn slowly to the chest while lying flat on his back on a blanket, and you ask him to keep a stool at the vat and sit between pours, however much he scorns it. He grumbles that stools are for women and bairns. Wren says something sharp from the rack, and he scowls and takes the stool.

Yes, there is a bonesetter. Mother Aldith keeps a house in Stonebridge, the market town a day's walk further down the valley past Greywater. She sets hips and the like, and is known for breaking and resetting bones that healed wrong, which is hard, but it is the only thing that will straighten his. Perrin says he will think on it, which, from a man like him, you take to mean maybe.

You have two 1st-level slots left. It is ten to two in the afternoon, and the village has been seen to. Wren is looking at you and the chapel and the road with a question in her face. Your prayers will come back by morning if you rest here, and Hollow Reach and the Lamp are a day behind you, with the road down to Stonebridge ahead.

What does Brannoc do?

I turn to Wren and kneel to her level. "You've done more than any one person should for Greywater, Wren. Let's sit in the chapel a moment, and I'll show you the dressing for Osric again and how to tell a fever from a chill, so there's someone here who knows."

I'll stay the night in Greywater, sweeping the chapel with her and keeping watch over Ilsa's baby, then rest to restore my prayers before heading down to Stonebridge. DM: does Mother Aldith have a reputation I should know of, and could I ask her to take on Wren as an apprentice?

In the chapel, Wren sits cross-legged on the cold flags with her yarn basket still beside her. She drinks it all in as if she were hungry for it. You show her Osric's dressing again, slowly, with your hands over hers: boiled water, honey thin, linen firm but not tight. You teach her the plain signs. A fever is hot, dry, and still. A chill shivers and sweats and comes and goes. A baby's breath is counted against a slow count of sixty, and blue at the lips is the thing you never wait on. She repeats each step back, and where she gets one wrong she says it again until it is right. You also teach her the first line of Edda's hymn, and she hums it badly and with great seriousness.

Your questions: Maud and Perrin both had something to say about Mother Aldith by the time you came for supper. She is blunt, loud, and short of patience for fools, and she is the best bonesetter in the valley. She has had three apprentices and two of them stayed. She wants coin from those who can pay, but never turns the poor from her door. Maud weaves her winter blankets, so she owes her a favour. Whether she'd take Wren is another matter, and one the dyer's daughter's parents must also answer. You write a short letter of recommendation in the margin of your prayer book and tear the leaf out. Wren holds it as if it were made of glass.

The evening goes on. You sweep the chapel with her, you set the kettle on for Ilsa, and you go twice to the low house on the east lane to count the baby's breaths against a slow sixty. Tessa sleeps easy on her mother's shoulder both times, the rattle looser than before.

It is nearly nine at night, and you have settled onto a pallet in the little chapel. Your prayers will return at dawn when you finish the long rest. You can change your prepared list then.

How does Brannoc spend the last of the evening, and which prayers does he prepare?

I spend the last of the evening kneeling at the plain stone altar, thanking the gods for Piper's mending, Osric's arm, and little Tessa's easy sleep, and humming Edda's hymn until Wren drowses off on the bench with her yarn basket in her lap. Then I lay out my pallet and let the long rest take me.

For tomorrow I'll keep my list as it is: Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready. I'll go down to Stonebridge in the morning to find Mother Aldith for Perrin and Wren, and keep my eyes open for the next place with no healer.

transcript.text: notebook: updated Greywater

You kneel at the altar a long while, and the words come without being sought, thanks for a boy who mends, for an arm that will keep its use, for a baby asleep against her mother. You hum until Wren's chin sinks to her chest and the yarn basket slides in her lap. You carry the basket to the bench beside her and lay your blanket over her shoulders. Then you lay out your pallet, the amulet in your fist, and the old stone chapel holds the night around you like a hand.

You wake at ten to five, before the first gray, rested and clear. Hit points 17 of 17, all three slots and your Channel Divinity restored, and both Hit Dice back. Your list is as you set it: Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready.

The chapel is cold and dim, with the first thin light at the window. Wren has curled up on the bench with your blanket, still asleep. Someone has left a small wooden bowl of porridge by the altar, still faintly warm, with a spoon across it and a twist of blue wool tied to the handle, Maud's mark. By the door, Osric, awake before dawn as weavers are, leans on the frame with his bandaged arm held against his chest, and gives you a nod that says more than he'd say aloud.

In the lane outside, the river is loud over the weir, and a single lamp is lit in Ilsa's window. Stonebridge is a day's walk down the valley. You carry the letter for Mother Aldith and Perrin's hip, and Wren's question, which is still unanswered. You can leave now, in the dark, or wait for the sun and Wren's waking.

What does Brannoc do?

I eat Maud's porridge standing by the altar, then wait for Wren to wake rather than slip away from her. When she stirs, I'll tell her I'm leaving for Stonebridge with her letter for Mother Aldith, and that her parents should hear it from her first before any road is chosen.

Before I go, I'll check Ilsa's baby once more by counting her breaths, and thank Osric for the nod. DM: is Wren's father or mother awake yet, and would they let me speak with them about the apprenticeship before I leave?

You eat Maud's porridge standing, warm all the way down, and wash the bowl at the chapel's well. You wait. It is not long. Wren stirs at the first full light, blinks at your blanket, and sits up in alarm as if she had overslept her own life. You tell her you are going to Stonebridge with her letter, and that her parents should hear it from her first, before any road is chosen. She goes very still, and then she nods hard and straightens her braid with both hands.

Before you go you count Tessa's breaths again, a slow sixty by the window. They are easy and even, her fist loose in her mother's hair. Ilsa, drowsy, mouths a thank you. You thank Osric, too, and his mouth twitches into something nearly a smile.

Her parents are already awake, as dyers are, and are already at the vats. The father, Corwin, is a large, quiet man with arms stained to the shoulder, and the mother, Hale, is quick and careful and does not stop working while she listens. You tell them plainly: that Wren has a mind for tending and a steady hand, that you have written to a bonesetter in Stonebridge on her behalf, that it is only a letter and a visit, and that the choice is theirs and hers.

Persuasion (19): they listen all through, and Hale is the one who asks the hard questions: how long, who feeds her, who keeps her safe, what happens if it is not a good fit. You answer honestly each time, including that you cannot promise it will suit. Corwin wipes his hands and says to the vat, not to you, "She's been sweeping that chapel since she was eight. Nobody asked her." At last they agree, on conditions: a one-month trial only, with Maud Marrow to go with her to Stonebridge when the weather holds, and a return at harvest if either of them wishes it. Wren holds her letter against her chest, and she does not cry, but she does not trust her voice.

It is twenty past six on Day 5. The village is waking, with smoke rising and the weir loud. You have all three prayers, a letter delivered, a hip to speak for, and the valley road down to Stonebridge, a day's walk, which you could take now.

What does Brannoc do?

I thank Corwin and Hale with a hand over my heart, then crouch to Wren. "A month's trial, and you can always come home. Keep up the dressings and the counting of breaths until Maud takes you down, and keep sweeping that chapel."

Then I shoulder my pack and set out down the valley road toward Stonebridge, to find Mother Aldith, speak for Perrin's hip, and see who else along the way has no healer. Wren stands straighter when you crouch to her. She says "Yes, sir," and then, after a moment, "Brannoc," and you both smile at it. She promises the dressings, the breath-counting, and the chapel, and she says it as one makes a vow. Corwin gives you a rough, sincere handclasp. Hale presses a twist of dried apple slices into your hand without looking up from the vat.

Your questions: Stonebridge is a day's walk by the valley road, about eight hours at a steady pace, and you will arrive in the afternoon. And yes, there is a house of your faith. It is a small hospice of twelve beds with a plain shrine, kept by a Brother Ansel, and under Shelter of the Faithful you and any companions can expect free healing and care there, provided you bring any material components yourself.

The road goes without trouble. The valley widens as you go, with the river broad and slow on your left. The fields are better kept, the fences are whole, and you pass a mill, a toll-hut with a bored keeper, and an ox-cart whose driver gives you a lift for two miles in exchange for a song, which you give him badly. You count the miles by the shadows.

At twenty past two the town rises out of the valley haze: Stonebridge, a walled huddle of timber and tile at the foot of a long stone bridge of seven arches. Carts queue at the gate, and drovers shout, and a bell somewhere rings the hour. Beyond the wall, over the roofs, you can see a bell-cote, a market cross, and a thin line of smoke from what must be a forge.

At the gate a guardsman in a patched tabard looks you over, the mace, the shield, the amulet, and waves you through with a tired "Healer? Hospice is past the tannery on the left. They'll be glad of you. We had a cart go over on the bridge this morning, three hurt, and Ansel's only got the two hands."

It is a little past two. You have your prayers, and the hospice is a short walk from the gate. Mother Aldith's house is somewhere in the town, and Perrin's hip is a promise you carry. What does Brannoc do?

"Then the hospice first. Three hurt from a cart can't wait on my errands."

I hurry past the tannery with my shield on my arm, find Brother Ansel, and say, "I'm Brannoc, a cleric of the Life domain, and I have three healing prayers ready. Tell me who is worst off and where to start." I'll triage by Medicine, put my Cure Wounds and Healing Word where they'll save the most, and ask about Mother Aldith once the wounded are settled.

You are through the gate and past the tannery in three minutes, and the hospice is easy to find: a low, long building of whitewashed timber, a plain shrine with a lamp burning at the end of it, and a green door standing open. Inside, Brother Ansel, a lean, gray, bright-eyed man in his sixties with a bandage roll in one hand and a bowl of water in the other, looks up and sees the amulet. "Edda's," he says. "I knew her, a long time ago. Gods bless her. Come, come."

You give your name and what you carry, three healing prayers, and he points with the bowl. Three cots, one apprentice, and no healer in the house but him.

Medicine (20, a natural 20): you move through the three of them with an ease that surprises you, and the whole picture comes clear in a minute.

Rudd Fenwick, the carter, has a shattered thigh and a steady, deep bleed through the dressing, and he is the worst off. Without help, he will not be alive by dark. Imma, an eleven-year-old girl who was riding with him, has a head knock, vomits, is drowsy and slow to answer, and should be watched through the night but is not in immediate danger. Tobin, a boy of nine, has a badly crushed ankle that will need Mother Aldith's setting, and he is shivering with shock.

And you notice what nobody else has. Round Tobin's ankle, under the swelling, are long gray finger-marks, four of them, spread wide, with a cold, blue-white burn at each tip like frost-bite. They smell faintly of the same sour grave-air as the hole at the Long Cut. The carter, half out of his head, keeps muttering that something pulled the wheel under the second arch. The horse bolted before the cart went over. The apprentice thinks he is raving.

You have three 1st-level slots, Cure Wounds and Healing Word both ready, and Channel Divinity's Preserve Life, with 10 hit points to divide among those at half their maximum or less. How do you spend them, and who do you ask about the bridge?

I go to Rudd first and cast Cure Wounds on him at 1st level, hand pressed over the dressing, to stop the bleed. Then I spend Preserve Life on Imma and Tobin, giving Imma 4 and Tobin 6 since the knock and the shock are what threaten them tonight, and I keep my last two slots in reserve for whatever the bridge has in store.

"Brother Ansel, those gray marks on Tobin's ankle are the same I saw in Hollow Reach. Ghouls. Who was on the bridge when it happened, and does anyone go under the second arch after dark? Please keep a lamp lit by every cot tonight."

Rudd first. You press your palm over the sodden dressing and the prayer takes, eight points of life going in, and under your hand the bleed slows, then stops. His gray face darkens to something living, and he draws a long, shuddering breath. The shattered thigh is still broken, but he will not die tonight.

Then Preserve Life, with the holy symbol held up and the light going out from it in a low gold wash over the two children's cots. Here the rules ask something of you. The channel can restore a creature only to half its hit point maximum and no further, and these children are small and badly hurt. Imma has little to give back, since her knock has taken her nearly to nothing, and so does Tobin. Between them, the prayer can restore only 3 points each, and the rest of its ten points find no place to go. It is less than you asked for, and it is what the rule allows. Imma's eyes clear and her vomiting stops. Tobin's shivering eases, and the blue goes from his lips. Neither is out of danger, but both are held.

Your Channel Divinity is spent until your next rest, and you have two 1st-level slots left.

Ansel answers your question over a basin, wringing a cloth. "Hodd Pell was the bridge-watchman this morning, and a dozen carters. I'll send the boy for him." He lowers his voice. "The second arch. There's an old river-stair under it, the Drowned Stair, down to a cellar-vault older than the bridge. Boatmen won't go under it after dark. Hodd says the lamp-oil goes missing from the arch niches, and he's heard something scratching on the wet stone. I thought it was rats." He looks at Tobin's ankle. "Gods keep us, I think I was wrong."

He does as you ask. By half past three there is a lamp lit by every cot, and a bowl of oil beside each, and his apprentice, a freckled boy named Pip, runs to fetch Hodd.

It is a quarter past three. The bridge is a short walk, the light is good, and the dark is about three hours off. You have two prayers left and no Channel Divinity, and a vault under the second arch that you have never seen.

What does Brannoc do?

I wait for Hodd Pell to arrive and sit with him by Rudd's cot. "Hodd, I'm Brannoc. Tell me everything you saw this morning, and how long the oil has been going missing from the niches. Have any boatmen or children gone near the Drowned Stair, and is the stair door locked or barred?"

Then I'll go look at the second arch in daylight, with Hodd and one or two of the town guard, and I'll do nothing hasty. I want to see the stair, the missing lamps and the marks, and then decide whether to seal it with iron and stone and light, as we did at the Long Cut.
